ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT Inspection | Greenville SC
ut.description: Ultrasonic testing in Greenville, SC: wall-thickness surveys and weld examination for plant piping, vessels and fabricated steel, mobilized to site. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Greenville, South Carolina
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT provides ultrasonic testing in Greenville, South Carolina and across the Upstate: wall-thickness surveys on piping, vessels and tanks, and angle-beam examination of welds in heavy fabrication, power equipment and plant structures. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope and report every reading against the code or specification you name. To request a quote, send your equipment list through the UT inspection quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Greenville

Greenville grew up on textile mills and now runs on advanced manufacturing, which changes the kind of steel that needs ultrasonic inspection. Instead of ship hulls and tank farms, the Upstate has factories: automotive plants and their suppliers around Spartanburg and Greenville, a large gas turbine assembly plant in Greenville, tire and chemical manufacturing, engineered-materials producers and aircraft production on the former Donaldson air base. All of them run steam, compressed air, process water and chemical piping, and all of them have heavy structural steel supporting production lines.

  • Utility and process piping: steam headers and condensate lines, a common legacy of mills converted to modern production, along with compressed air, hot oil and chemical service lines.
  • Boilers and pressure vessels: package boilers, air receivers, reactors, autoclaves and heat exchangers in plants that cure, mold or process material under pressure.
  • Heavy fabrication: thick weldments for power equipment, where the weld volume must be sound before the part ships to a power plant, data center or gas export terminal.
  • Structural steel: crane runways, press foundations, building frames and highway bridge steel along the I-85 corridor.

Ultrasonic work here tends to be planned around production schedules rather than ship calls, so the ability to work around operating lines matters more than outage speed.

What ultrasonic testing finds and what it misses

The technique launches short pulses of sound into the metal and listens for echoes. In a thickness survey, the time between the front surface and the back wall converts to remaining wall. In a weld examination, an echo that arrives between the surfaces points to a reflector, and its timing and height indicate where it is and how large it is. UT therefore reveals internal conditions that a surface method cannot: general thinning, lamination, inclusion, lack of fusion, incomplete penetration and cracks that do not break the surface.

Limits are real and should be stated in the quote. Sound does not travel well across air gaps, so rough, scaled or poorly coupled surfaces reduce accuracy. Cast iron, thick castings and austenitic weld metal scatter the beam and need a qualified technique. Flaws shaped like a flat plane aligned with the beam can be missed, so welds are examined from both sides and from more than one angle. Very thin sections have a dead zone near the surface where the instrument cannot separate echoes, and a probe designed for thin material is needed.

Codes and acceptance criteria

ASME Section V provides the examination rules: Article 4 for welds, Article 5 for materials, and the thickness measurement practice in SE-797, which sits in Article 23. ASTM E797 and ASTM E164 cover contact thickness measurement and contact examination of weldments in general industry. Acceptance criteria are set elsewhere. ASME B31.3 governs process piping, and its ultrasonic provisions and Table 341.3.2 set the limits. ASME B31.1 applies to power piping. Welds on pressure vessels follow ASME Section VIII Division 1, where Appendix 12 sets ultrasonic acceptance. Structural groove welds fall under AWS D1.1, and AWS D1.5 covers steel bridges, which matters for the DOT work along the Interstate corridors.

Once equipment is in service, owners usually run API 510 for vessels, API 570 for piping or API 653 for tanks. These programs make the owner's authorized inspector responsible for the inspection; Atlantis supplies the ultrasonic measurements and flags readings approaching minimum so the inspector can calculate remaining life and next inspection date. Under OSHA's 29 CFR 1910.119(j), plants covered by process safety management must also keep mechanical integrity inspection records.

In South Carolina the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act, found in Title 41, Chapter 14 of the state code, is administered by the Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation. It recognizes ASME and National Board stamped equipment, and repairs or alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code. A weld flaw found by ultrasonic testing on a stamped vessel normally leads to a repair procedure under that code.

Technique in practice

For thickness work, the technician starts from your drawing or isometric and the condition monitoring locations marked on it. Each location is cleaned, coupled with gel or paste, and measured with a dual-element probe, the style of probe designed for corroded and pitted walls. The instrument is calibrated on a step block of the same alloy before the first reading and verified at intervals. Where a wall is thin, pitted or lined, the technician reads the A-scan and not only the number, because a gauge reporting only a digit can lock onto a lamination or a double echo and give a thickness that looks fine. High-temperature work uses a special probe and couplant, with a correction for the temperature of the metal.

For welds, a typical setup uses an angle-beam probe at 45, 60 or 70 degrees. The technician builds a distance-amplitude curve using side-drilled holes in a calibration block of the same material and thickness range, raises the scanning gain above the reference level, and moves the probe back and forth across the weld while skewing the beam to cover the fusion faces and root. Indications are measured for location, length and amplitude and then judged against the governing acceptance table.

Who performs the work

Atlantis technicians are qualified by the company under a written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians set up the equipment, run the examination and interpret results; an ASNT NDT Level III approves the procedures and reviews the reports. The procedure for a Greenville job names the code edition, the calibration blocks, the scan plan and the evaluation criteria. If your own procedures need a second pair of eyes, the outsourced Level III consulting page describes how that review works.

What the ultrasonic report contains

  • Identification of each component with drawing or isometric reference, material and nominal wall, and the locations examined.
  • Procedure number and revision, code edition and acceptance criteria applied.
  • Instrument, probes, wedges, couplant and calibration blocks, with calibration checks recorded at the start, during and at the end of the job.
  • For thickness work, a table or grid of readings that highlights the thinnest locations and any reading below the stated minimum.
  • For welds, a list of indications with position, length, amplitude, evaluation and a sketch of the weld showing where each one sits.
  • Technician name and certification level, date and Level III review.

Readings that reach the minimum are called out to your inspector immediately, not left for the final document.

Planning an ultrasonic job in Greenville

Upstate weather is milder than the Gulf Coast but not trivial. Summers are warm and humid, with about forty days a year at or above 90 degrees Fahrenheit, which makes roof-top piping and sun-heated tanks too warm for ordinary couplant and probes. Winters bring around fifty nights below freezing, and occasional ice storms can close roads and interrupt travel. Exterior surveys planned for January should include a weather window, and gel couplant stiffens in the cold.

Plants in the Upstate typically require contractor orientation, badging and lock-out coordination, and production lines may only be accessible during planned shutdowns. Atlantis has no office in Greenville, so technicians are mobilized to your site and travel along the Interstate network, with Greenville-Spartanburg airport the nearest commercial gateway. Include crew mobilization in your shutdown plan rather than assuming same-week arrival.

UT, MT or PT for your Greenville job

Choose ultrasonic testing when the question concerns wall loss, internal weld quality or the depth of a flaw. For surface cracks in carbon steel welds, magnetic particle inspection in Greenville is faster. For stainless steel, aluminum and other non-magnetic alloys, liquid penetrant testing in Greenville finds surface-breaking cracks. Many scopes combine methods: a thickness survey across a piping system, followed by MT or PT of the repair welds. The overview of ultrasonic testing services and the ultimate guide to UT give more background, and the Article 5 requirements page covers thickness measurement under the code.

Training your own ultrasonic technicians

Greenville manufacturers that run their own maintenance and quality teams often prefer to certify their own technicians. The UT Level 1 course and UT Level 2 course cover theory, technique and documentation, and the ultrasonic simulator gives trainees practice before they touch a calibration block. Practical hours and examinations happen at your facility under your written practice, since the employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A. The Greenville training page explains how courses are arranged locally.

faq.q: What kinds of Greenville facilities need ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Manufacturing plants with steam, compressed air or chemical piping, boilers and pressure vessels, heavy fabrication shops, and structural steel such as crane runways and bridge members. We measure wall thickness and examine welds on the components your program lists.

faq.q: Can UT measure thickness through paint?
faq.a: Often yes. With a suitable instrument and probe, readings can be taken through intact coating, and the coating thickness is accounted for. Loose, blistered or thick coating degrades coupling, so those areas may need local removal before measurement.

faq.q: Does ultrasonic testing replace radiography on welds?
faq.a: Some codes permit ultrasonic examination of production welds as an alternative, including provisions in ASME B31.3 and AWS D1.1. Substitution has to be agreed with the owner, engineer and authorized inspector before the work starts, and it is not automatic.

faq.q: What is a condition monitoring location?
faq.a: A condition monitoring location is a specific point on a pipe, vessel or tank where thickness is measured repeatedly over the life of the equipment. Repeating readings at the same spot lets the inspector calculate corrosion rate and remaining life.

faq.q: How accurate are ultrasonic thickness readings?
faq.a: Accuracy depends on calibration, surface condition and the probe. With a calibrated instrument and a clean surface, readings are consistent to a small fraction of a millimeter. Rough or pitted surfaces reduce accuracy, which the report notes.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Greenville?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Greenville. Qualified technicians are mobilized to your plant or yard for the agreed scope, and the report is reviewed by an ASNT NDT Level III before it is issued to you.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects what you find?
faq.a: The governing code sets the criteria, and for equipment under API 510, 570 or 653 your authorized inspector makes the call. We report measured data and flag anything near the minimum so you can act on it without delay.

faq.q: Can you examine thick-wall weldments for power equipment?
faq.a: Yes, within the limits of the material and geometry. Thick sections and austenitic welds may require a specific probe and calibration block, so provide material, thickness and the governing code when requesting a quote.

faq.q: How do our staff qualify as ultrasonic technicians?
faq.a: Sign them up for Level 1 and Level 2 UT training, practice on the simulator, then complete practical hours and exams at your plant under your written practice. The employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A, with your Level III approving the process.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Greenville, SC
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection in Greenville, SC for weld cracks on fabricated steel, press frames, cranes, shafts and forgings, mobilized to site. Request a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Greenville, South Carolina
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs magnetic particle inspection (MPI) in Greenville, South Carolina, examining carbon and low-alloy steel for surface and slightly subsurface cracks. Typical jobs include welds on fabricated equipment, press and machine frames, crane runways and hooks, shafts, gears and forgings. Technicians are mobilized to your plant. Send the part or weld list through the MT inspection quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle testing is used in Greenville

The Upstate makes things out of steel, and things that are made and run hard crack. Greenville has a large gas turbine assembly plant, automotive and tire plants with stamping and molding equipment, bearing and gear producers, and engineered-materials makers whose lines run on heavy frames and shafts. Military and commercial aircraft work at the former Donaldson air base adds tooling and ground equipment. The I-85 corridor connects all of this to a rail-served inland port at Greer, whose cranes and rail-mounted equipment are steel structures in their own right.

  • Fabrication and machining: weld toes, root repairs, crater cracks and heat-treated parts, examined before they leave the shop or return to service.
  • Press lines and machine frames: tie rods, crown and bed welds, and large pins and bolting exposed to cyclic stress.
  • Cranes and runways: overhead crane girders, hooks, trolley frames and the welds on runway brackets.
  • Drive trains: shafts, couplings, gears and splines in plants where a failure takes a line down.

What magnetic particle testing finds and what it misses

MT applies to ferromagnetic metals: carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic or ferritic stainless grades. Austenitic stainless, aluminum, brass and titanium are not magnetic, so those parts need a different surface method. When a magnetic field passes through a sound part, it stays inside the metal; at a crack that crosses the field, the lines leak out and attract fine iron particles, which pile up along the crack and make it visible. Surface-breaking cracks give crisp indications, and very shallow subsurface flaws on smooth parts can show as softer, broader lines.

The method has limits. It gives no depth, so a crack's severity may need ultrasonic or grinding follow-up. It does not find flaws more than a short distance beneath the surface. Coatings and scale hold the particles away from the metal. And since cracks parallel to the field produce no flux leakage, each area is examined twice with the field rotated about ninety degrees, so any crack direction is covered.

Codes and acceptance criteria

ASME Section V Article 7 defines how MT is performed, covering equipment, particle materials, field strength, lighting and documentation. ASTM E1444 is the common practice standard and ASTM E709 the guide that explains the method. Acceptance comes from the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 sets MT methods and acceptance in Mandatory Appendix 6, ASME B31.3 addresses magnetic particle examination at paragraph 344.3 with limits in Table 341.3.2, ASME B31.1 applies to power piping, and AWS D1.1 and D1.5 cover welded structures and bridges. In many Upstate shops, the customer's own drawing note or purchase specification adds extra requirements, such as fluorescent particles or a maximum background level, and these take precedence in the procedure.

South Carolina regulates boilers and pressure vessels under the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act in Title 41, Chapter 14, administered by the Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation. The National Board Inspection Code governs repairs and alterations, and weld repairs normally call for MT or PT of the excavation and finished weld. In service, owners operating under API 510, 570 or 653 depend on their authorized inspector to accept the repair; Atlantis supplies the examination and the record.

Technique: yokes, prods and particles

Most field work uses a handheld electromagnetic yoke. The code requires an AC yoke to lift at least 10 pounds at the largest pole spacing used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke to lift at least 40 pounds; the technician checks lifting power with a test weight on a schedule. The poles are placed on both sides of the weld, particles are applied dry or in a liquid suspension while the field is on, and the technician looks for lines of particles that gather at a discontinuity. After the first pass the yoke is turned about ninety degrees and the examination repeated.

Contact prods pass current into the part and reach inside corners the yoke cannot, but they can burn the surface, so many specifications limit or prohibit them. Visible particles in a contrast color are the standard for field work. Wet fluorescent particles give higher sensitivity and are observed under UV-A light in a darkened enclosure; they are common on shafts, gears and critical machined parts. After examination, the technician checks residual magnetism and demagnetizes the part if leftover fields would disturb welding, machining or service.

Common findings in Upstate manufacturing steel

In fabricated structures, MT frequently finds toe cracks and crater cracks at weld terminations. In heavy sections welded without adequate preheat, hydrogen cracking can appear hours or days after welding. In rotating equipment the finding is often a fatigue crack that started at a keyway, a fillet or a threaded section, and in heat-treated parts it can be quench or grinding cracks. Machining marks, scratches and sharp geometry changes can mimic cracks, so indications are cleaned and re-examined before they are recorded.

When an indication is confirmed, the report says where it is and how long it is. Depth has to be established another way, either by controlled grinding followed by re-examination or by ultrasonic measurement, and the owner's engineer decides whether the part is repaired or retired.

Who performs the work

MT is carried out by technicians qualified by Atlantis under its written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up the equipment, performs the examination and interprets what is found. An ASNT NDT Level III approves the written procedure and reviews each report. The procedure names the code, the magnetizing method, the particle type and the lighting, so the Greenville examination follows what the specification says. For help with your own procedures, the written practice development page describes the service.

What the MT report contains

  • Component or weld identification, material, surface condition and examined areas.
  • Procedure number and revision, code edition and acceptance criteria.
  • Magnetizing method, current type, yoke lifting test, particle type and carrier, and light levels for fluorescent work.
  • Each relevant indication with location, length and orientation, with a sketch or photograph and an accept or reject decision.
  • Demagnetization performed and the residual field measured.
  • Technician name and level, date and the Level III review.

Planning a magnetic particle job in Greenville

Upstate weather rarely stops MT, but it affects the plan. Summer days can pass 90 degrees Fahrenheit, and hot steel can dry wet particles too quickly or damage contrast paint, so shaded work or early starts help. Winters bring freezing nights and ice storms; cold steel is fine for magnetic particle, but wet suspensions can thicken and the technician's hands need heated gloves. Fluorescent work outdoors needs a tent or dark area, since daylight overwhelms the lamp.

Manufacturing plants have contractor orientation, lock-out and hot-work rules, and crane or press inspection needs the equipment out of production. Atlantis has no office in Greenville, so crews travel to your facility; arrange access and downtime before they mobilize, and confirm whether you need escort, a manlift or scaffolding for overhead structures.

MT, PT or UT for your Greenville job

MT is the first choice for surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel. If the part is stainless steel, aluminum or another non-magnetic metal, use dye penetrant inspection in Greenville. If you need to know how deep a crack goes or whether the inside of a weld is sound, use ultrasonic inspection in Greenville. The overview of magnetic particle testing services, the complete MT guide and the Article 7 requirements explain the method and the code side in more detail.

Training your own magnetic particle technicians

Greenville plants that inspect their own fabrications or maintain their own cranes often qualify in-house technicians. The MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 courses cover the theory and the practical skills, and the NDT practice tests help trainees prepare. The Greenville NDT training page explains local delivery, and practical qualification is completed at your facility under your written practice.

faq.q: Which Greenville parts suit magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: Carbon and low-alloy steel parts that see stress or have been welded: fabricated frames, crane hooks and girders, press components, shafts, gears and forgings. Stainless steel and aluminum cannot be magnetized and need penetrant testing.

faq.q: Can MPI be done on painted steel?
faq.a: A thin, tightly bonded coating may be acceptable if the procedure allows it, but thick, flaking or conductive coatings hide cracks. Most specifications call for bare metal or a controlled thin coating at the examination areas.

faq.q: When should we use fluorescent instead of visible particles?
faq.a: Choose fluorescent when the specification requires it, when cracks are fine or tight, or when parts are machined. They need UV-A light and a dark area, while visible particles on contrast paint work in normal light.

faq.q: Why is each area examined twice?
faq.a: A crack only produces a strong indication when it crosses the magnetic field. By repeating the examination with the field turned roughly ninety degrees, cracks running in any direction are covered by at least one pass.

faq.q: Do examined parts need demagnetizing?
faq.a: If a residual field could affect welding, machining, instruments or later service, the part is demagnetized and the remaining field is measured. The procedure states the requirement and the acceptable residual level.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Greenville?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Greenville. Technicians are mobilized to your plant for the agreed scope, and an ASNT NDT Level III reviews the report before it is issued.

faq.q: What do you need from us before the visit?
faq.a: A list of parts or welds with drawings, material types, the code or customer specification, access arrangements, safety and orientation requirements, and any temperature limits that apply to the surfaces.

faq.q: Can MT be used on hot parts?
faq.a: Only within the temperature range the procedure is qualified for. Wet particles and contrast paints have limits, so hot parts must cool or the procedure must be qualified for the higher temperature.

faq.q: How do Greenville companies train their own MT technicians?
faq.a: Enroll staff in MT Level 1 and Level 2 training, then complete practical examination on site under your written practice. The employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A, and your Level III approves the practical.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing in Greenville, SC | Dye PT
pt.description: Dye penetrant inspection in Greenville, SC for stainless, aluminum and steel welds, machined parts, vessels and piping, mobilized to your site. Request a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Greenville, South Carolina
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs liquid penetrant testing, often called dye penetrant inspection, in Greenville, South Carolina. It reveals surface-breaking cracks, porosity and laps in stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys, titanium and carbon steel, and it suits the machined parts, welded assemblies and corrosion-resistant equipment found across the Upstate. Technicians travel to your plant. Request a quote through the PT inspection quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in Greenville

Penetrant is the surface method for everything a magnet cannot handle, and Greenville produces a great deal of it. Gas turbine components and power equipment use alloy steels and nickel alloys; chemical and engineered-materials plants run stainless piping, reactors and heat exchangers; food and consumer-product plants use sanitary stainless tanks and lines; and aerospace and medical-device work uses aluminum, titanium and stainless machined parts. Automotive suppliers machine and weld aluminum and steel components where a surface crack in a weld or casting can cause a field failure.

  • Stainless and alloy welds: root and cap passes on process piping, nozzles and tube-to-tubesheet joints in corrosive service.
  • Machined and cast parts: housings, impellers, valve bodies and turbine-related components examined for cracks and porosity open to the surface.
  • Aluminum fabrications: welded frames, tanks and enclosures where magnetic methods cannot be used.
  • Repairs: excavations after crack removal and the finished weld, before the equipment goes back into service.

What penetrant testing finds and what it misses

PT works on the same principle as a stain on a cloth: a thin liquid soaks into any opening at the surface and is pulled out again by a developer, so the opening appears as a colored or glowing line. Cracks, laps, seams, cold shuts and open porosity all show. The method does not depend on the metal being magnetic, so it is the standard choice for stainless steel, aluminum and nickel alloys.

It does not see anything below the surface. A void inside a weld, wall thinning or an internal crack is invisible to penetrant, and a surface that has been smeared closed by grinding, peening or machining can hide cracks that are really there. Porous surfaces absorb liquid and make the background glow. Paint, oil, rust and flux fill defects and prevent penetrant from entering them, which is why cleaning before the test is as important as the test itself.

Codes and acceptance criteria

ASME Section V Article 6 defines the process steps and controls, and ASTM E165 is the common practice for general-industry parts. Acceptance depends on the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 puts penetrant methods and acceptance in Mandatory Appendix 8, ASME B31.3 covers liquid penetrant examination at paragraph 344.4 with limits in Table 341.3.2, and AWS D1.1, D1.5 and D1.6 cover welded structures, bridges and stainless steel. Customer drawing notes often set the sensitivity level or the penetrant family, and the procedure then follows them.

For stainless and nickel alloys, specifications commonly limit halogens and sulfur in the penetrant materials. Lot certificates are kept in the job record. In South Carolina, stamped boilers and pressure vessels fall under the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act and its administering agency, the Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation, with repairs following the National Board Inspection Code. For in-service equipment under API 510, 570 or 653, the owner's authorized inspector accepts or rejects results.

Technique: step by step

The surface is cleaned first. Loose scale and spatter are removed mechanically, then solvent cleaning takes off oil and residue, and the surface is allowed to dry. Penetrant, either visible red dye or fluorescent, is sprayed or brushed on and left to dwell for the time in the procedure. Excess is removed using the system the procedure specifies: solvent wipe, water wash, or an emulsifier followed by water. A thin, even coat of developer goes on, and the technician evaluates indications after the development time, reading visible dye in good white light and fluorescent indications under UV-A in a dark enclosure.

The standard temperature range for the part and materials is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Below or above it, the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature with a comparator block. Cold parts slow penetrant entry, and hot parts let the liquid evaporate before it works.

Choosing a penetrant system for Upstate work

Field work in Greenville plants generally favors solvent-removable visible-dye penetrant because it needs no water supply or drain and leaves little waste. Fluorescent systems are chosen for machined components, critical welds and tight cracks, and they need a darkened enclosure. Water-washable systems suit large production batches in a shop with a wash station. The system affects sensitivity, cleanup effort and cost of the job, so the procedure fixes it for each scope, and the report names the brand and lot of every material used.

Common findings with penetrant testing

On welds, penetrant most often finds crater cracks, toe cracks, surface porosity and lack of fusion at the surface. On castings and machined parts it shows shrinkage cracks, laps, seams and grinding cracks. In service, it finds fatigue cracks and, in stainless equipment, stress corrosion cracking, which can be tight and need careful cleaning to reveal.

False indications are also routine. Surface roughness, scratches, weld spatter and incomplete removal of excess penetrant look like flaws. The technician wipes the spot, applies developer again and looks once more. Real cracks bleed back in the same place; false indications fade. Only persistent indications are measured and recorded.

Who performs the work

Penetrant examination is carried out by technicians qualified by the company under a written practice that follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician controls each step, performs the examination and evaluates results. An ASNT NDT Level III approves the procedure and reviews each report. Procedures for Greenville jobs specify the penetrant system, dwell times, temperature range and acceptance code. If you need help developing a written practice or procedure, the Level III consulting page explains the service.

What the PT report contains

  • Component or weld identification, material and the areas examined.
  • Procedure number and revision, code edition, acceptance criteria and sensitivity level.
  • Penetrant, remover and developer brands and lot numbers, with halogen and sulfur certificates for stainless and nickel alloys.
  • Surface temperature, pre-clean method, dwell time and development time.
  • Each relevant indication with location, size and type, recorded by sketch or photograph, with an accept or reject decision.
  • Technician name and level, date and the Level III review.

Planning a penetrant job in Greenville

Greenville's seasons matter for penetrant. Summer afternoons above 90 degrees Fahrenheit take steel beyond the 125 degree limit when it is in direct sun, so shade or early shifts avoid requalifying the process. Winter nights below freezing slow the liquid, and ice storms can disrupt travel and outdoor work, so cold-weather jobs call for a heated enclosure. Humid air slows drying after cleaning, and a damp crack will not accept penetrant, so allow drying time. Wind and rain require a tent for outdoor surfaces.

Plants require contractor orientation, chemical approvals and often a permit for solvents. Atlantis has no office in Greenville, so crews travel to your facility; the schedule should cover access, safety orientation and chemical-handling approvals before mobilization.

PT, MT or UT for your Greenville job

Penetrant is the right choice for non-magnetic metals and for surface cracks on complex shapes. For carbon steel where speed and sensitivity at the surface matter, use magnetic particle inspection in Greenville. When you need to look inside the wall or weld, use ultrasonic testing in Greenville. The overview of liquid penetrant testing services, the Article 6 explainer and the MT versus PT comparison give more detail on selection and the code.

Training your own penetrant technicians

Penetrant testing is a practical entry point for in-house inspection staff. The PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training courses cover the process and the code, and the penetrant simulator lets trainees repeat the process steps. Qualification is completed on site under your written practice, and the Greenville training page explains how courses are arranged.

faq.q: What materials can liquid penetrant testing inspect?
faq.a: Any non-porous material, including stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys, titanium, copper alloys and carbon steel. It finds only flaws open to the surface, so internal weld defects need ultrasonic testing.

faq.q: Is dye penetrant or fluorescent penetrant better?
faq.a: Neither is better in every case. Visible dye works in normal light and suits most field jobs, while fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive to fine cracks and is needed when a specification requires it.

faq.q: Why must surfaces be cleaned before the test?
faq.a: Oil, paint, scale and flux fill cracks, and grinding or machining can smear metal over them. If penetrant cannot enter a crack, the crack cannot be found, so cleaning and drying are part of the examination.

faq.q: What temperature limits apply to PT?
faq.a: The standard range is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit under ASME Section V Article 6. Outside that range the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature, so hot or frozen parts need extra planning.

faq.q: Why are halogen limits used on stainless steel?
faq.a: Chlorides and fluorides can cause cracking in stainless and nickel alloys during service or heat treatment. Low-contaminant materials are used on those metals, and the lot certificates are kept with the job record.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Greenville?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Greenville. Technicians are mobilized to your plant for the agreed scope, and an ASNT NDT Level III reviews each report before it is issued to you.

faq.q: Can penetrant find cracks below the surface?
faq.a: No. It only shows flaws that are open to the surface. Internal flaws need ultrasonic testing, and subsurface cracks in carbon steel may show with magnetic particle inspection.

faq.q: How are doubtful indications handled?
faq.a: The area is wiped, cleaned and developed again. Real cracks bleed back in the same place while false indications fade, and only persistent indications are recorded for your inspector's decision.

faq.q: How can Greenville employers qualify penetrant technicians?
faq.a: Enroll staff in PT Level 1 and Level 2 training, practice on the simulator, then complete practical examination on site under your written practice. The employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A.
